title: Pre-treatment for real-time bacterial counting in water
text:
2018 – 2020
Full title: Development of pre-treatment for real-time bacterial counting (リアルタイム微生物計測に対する前処理手法の開発)
Topics: microbial water quality · wastewater treatment · membrane filtration · online monitoring
My contributions: experimental design, pre-treatment system operation, fluorescence and bacterial analysis
Skills used: ion exchange, diafiltration, fluorescence spectrophotometry, online bacteriological counting, epifluorescence microscopy

title: Pre-treatment for real-time bacterial counting in water
text:
Thesis at a glance







Degree
MEng in Water and Environmental Engineering


Programme
Integrated Engineering, International Water Environmental Engineering Course, Nagasaki University


Completed
July 2020


Water tested
MBR-treated wastewater and river water


Key result
Diafiltration with a 10 kDa membrane (from 4 diafiltration volumes) enabled error-free online bacterial counting

title: Pre-treatment for real-time bacterial counting in water
text:
Why it matters
Safe water depends on knowing how many bacteria remain after treatment. Common methods such as Heterotrophic Plate Count (HPC) and Flow Cytometry (FCM) work well, but they are not suited to continuous, long-term monitoring.
Real-time bacterial counting can monitor water continuously, but it has a weak spot: dissolved organic matter, especially humic acid-like substances, gives off fluorescence that interferes with the measurement. This thesis set out to remove those interfering substances while keeping the bacteria, so they can still be counted accurately.

title: Pre-treatment for real-time bacterial counting in water
text:
What I did
I developed and compared two pre-treatment methods:
1. Fluidized bed ion exchange

An ion exchange column (Φ18 × 300 mm) filled with commercial anion exchange resin A860
MBR-treated wastewater and river water pumped upward through the resin at 40 mL/min

2. Diafiltration

Membranes with two molecular weight cut-offs: 10 kDa and 50 kDa
Water concentrated at 40 mL/min and 2 bar, then diluted back with buffer, repeated for 3, 4, 5 and 6 diafiltration volumes (DVs)

All treated samples were analysed with a fluorescence spectrophotometer, an online bacteriological counting system and epifluorescence microscopy.

title: Pre-treatment for real-time bacterial counting in water
text:
Key findings

Ion exchange works for river water, not for wastewater



Fluorescence of interfering substances before and after ion exchange with resin A860 (Ex 405 nm)



Treated river water reached low fluorescence (below 100) and could be counted online
Treated MBR wastewater still showed high fluorescence (around 400), too high for online counting



Diafiltration with a 10 kDa membrane is the winner



Fluorescence after diafiltration with 10 kDa (orange) and 50 kDa (grey) membranes



The 10 kDa membrane removed far more interfering substances than the 50 kDa membrane
From 4 diafiltration volumes onwards, treated wastewater could be counted online without errors




Stable real-time bacterial counts after diafiltration with the 10 kDa membrane (4, 5 and 6 DVs)

title: Pre-treatment for real-time bacterial counting in water
text:
Conclusion
Both methods reduced dissolved organic matter in MBR-treated wastewater, but only diafiltration with a 10 kDa membrane removed enough interfering substances for reliable real-time counting. This makes it a promising pre-treatment step to support continuous microbial monitoring in water and wastewater treatment.

title: Sustainable conversion of CO₂ into cyclic organic carbonates
text:
Thesis at a glance







Degree
MSc in Sustainable Development, with Distinction


Institution
University Centre for Environmental Studies and Sustainable Development, University of Warsaw


Supervisor
Dr. hab. Elżbieta Megiel, Associate Professor, Faculty of Chemistry, University of Warsaw


Completed
July 2026


Best result
99.8% conversion and 71.3% yield of styrene carbonate

title: Sustainable conversion of CO₂ into cyclic organic carbonates
text:
Why it matters
CO₂ is the main greenhouse gas, and switching to renewable energy alone is not enough to bring emissions down. Carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) offers a complementary route: treating CO₂ as a raw material instead of waste.
One of the most promising CCU products are cyclic organic carbonates (COCs), used in batteries, green solvents and polymers. They are usually made from CO₂ and epoxides, which are toxic. A cleaner alternative is oxidative carboxylation: starting from cheaper, safer olefins and converting them to carbonates in a single “one-pot” process. This requires a catalyst that can do two jobs at once.

title: Sustainable conversion of CO₂ into cyclic organic carbonates
text:
What I did
I designed and synthesised a new tandem catalyst combining two types of active sites on one support:

Multiwalled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs), a support material that can be produced from organic waste, functionalised with tetrazolium–bromide groups to drive CO₂ cycloaddition
Silver nanoparticles stabilised with polyethyleneimine (AgNPs•PEI) to drive the epoxidation step




SEM image of the carbon-nanotube catalyst material (scale bar 100 nm)


I then tested the catalyst on two model reactions, using styrene oxide and styrene, under mild conditions (70–100 °C, 1–26 bar CO₂), with and without a co-catalyst (TBAB).



Study workflow: two reaction routes tested with the new tandem catalyst

title: Sustainable conversion of CO₂ into cyclic organic carbonates
text:
Key findings



Conversion and yield across all catalytic tests. Best results highlighted in red.



CO₂ + styrene oxide: up to 99.8% conversion and 71.3% yield of styrene carbonate (71.5% selectivity) at 100 °C and 25 bar, competitive with other heterogeneous catalysts reported to date
One-pot route from styrene: high conversion (up to 91%) but low carbonate yield (below 5%), showing that selectivity, not conversion, is the bottleneck
The co-catalyst is essential: adding TBAB raised the average yield from 0.5% to 29.3%; without it, yields stayed near zero regardless of temperature or pressure
Catalyst design matters: placing separate active sites on one support can reduce selectivity, pointing future work towards better-integrated catalyst designs

title: Sustainable conversion of CO₂ into cyclic organic carbonates
text:
Next steps

Test the catalyst variant with higher-molecular-weight PEI (PEI-25k)
Quantify by-products such as benzaldehyde by GC
Use a two-temperature programme in the one-pot system: lower for epoxidation, higher for cycloaddition
Test other oxidants (O₂, H₂O₂) and assess catalyst recyclability over multiple cycles

title: Sustainable conversion of CO₂ into cyclic organic carbonates
text:
Outcomes

Review paper
The literature research in this thesis contributes to a review paper:

Megiel, E., Pham, H. T. Polymer-based advanced catalytic systems for the thermal conversion of CO₂ into five-membered cyclic organic carbonates: A comprehensive review. Journal of CO₂ Utilization. Under revision, 2026.



Conference presentation

Megiel, E., Wasiluk, K., Kopacka, G., Pham, H. T., Gungor, S. (2026). Sustainable catalytic conversion of CO₂ to cyclic organic carbonates using hybrid nanomaterials.

Keywords: CO₂ fixation · cyclic organic carbonates · oxidative carboxylation · CO₂ cycloaddition · tandem catalyst · multiwalled carbon nanotubes · silver nanoparticles · styrene carbonate · heterogeneous catalysis

title: Advanced oxidation processes for industrial wastewater reuse
text:
Why it matters
Le Minh Xuan Industrial Park hosts highly polluting industries such as textile dyeing, electroplating, tanning and pesticide production. Its central treatment plant (4,000 m³/day) uses biological treatment, but the effluent still carried high colour and residual organic matter that biological processes cannot break down. That water was discharged to nearby canals, affecting residents.
Advanced oxidation processes generate hydroxyl radicals (•OH), one of the strongest oxidants in water treatment. They can degrade pollutants that biological treatment leaves behind. The thesis asked which AOP could polish this effluent to meet discharge standards and support water reuse.

title: Advanced oxidation processes for industrial wastewater reuse
text:
What I did

Built and operated four lab-scale AOP systems on sand-filtered secondary effluent (inlet COD about 90 ± 10 mg/L):

Ozone alone (O₃)
Ozone with UV (O₃/UV)
UV photocatalysis (UV/TiO₂)
Combined O₃/UV/TiO₂

Optimised operating conditions step by step: pH, ozone dose (mg O₃/mg COD), UV dose and TiO₂ loading
Prepared a reusable photocatalyst by dip-coating TiO₂/PEG onto crushed recycled car-window glass (2–3 mm beads), followed by calcination at 550 °C
Measured residual and reacted ozone to calculate ozone use efficiency
Compared all four systems with one-way ANOVA and post hoc tests
Weighed treatment performance against operating complexity, equipment and chemical costs to recommend a full-scale option

title: Advanced oxidation processes for industrial wastewater reuse
text:
Key findings









Process
Optimal conditions
COD removal
Colour removal




O₃ alone
pH 9, 0.9 mg O₃/mg COD
32%
71%


O₃/UV
pH 9, 1.2 mg O₃/mg COD, UV 1.6 Ws/cm²
53%
69%


UV/TiO₂
neutral pH, 1 g/L TiO₂, UV 1.6 Ws/cm²
40%
43%


O₃/UV/TiO₂
pH 9, 1.2 mg O₃/mg COD, 1 g/L TiO₂, UV 1.6 Ws/cm²
55%
74%




The combined O₃/UV/TiO₂ system removed the most COD and colour, and differences in COD removal between all four systems were statistically significant.
For colour, ozone-based systems performed similarly to each other and far better than UV/TiO₂.
After weighing cost, equipment and ease of operation, ozone alone was recommended as the most practical polishing step. Its effluent met Vietnam’s industrial discharge standard (QCVN 40:2011/BTNMT, Level B).

title: Advanced oxidation processes for industrial wastewater reuse
text:
Next steps

Develop the O₃/UV/TiO₂ system further so its higher removal comes at a viable cost
Test longer ozonation times (1, 3, 6 hours) to track how far pollutant removal can go
Improve ozone use efficiency, which was only 56–70%, for example by recovering off-gas ozone
Assess removal of toxic compounds (pesticides, heavy metals) and pathogens in ozone-based systems

title: Advanced oxidation processes for industrial wastewater reuse
text:
Outcomes

Publication
The thesis results were published as a research article:
Pham, H. T., Thai, M. Q., Nguyen, T. T., Dinh, L. M., Phan, T. H. V., Vo, T. H., & Bui, X. T. (2014). Influence of advanced oxidation processes (AOPs) on COD and color removal in secondary industrial effluent. Journal of Vietnam Academy of Science and Technology, VOLUME(ISSUE), PAGES. DOI/link

title: Street-level carbon footprint of urban transport in Poland
text:
Why it matters
Transport is one of the main sources of greenhouse gas emissions in cities, and adding road capacity often brings more traffic and more emissions. Planners need to know where emissions concentrate so they can act on the right streets. The Institute’s existing Excel-based inventory focused mainly on cars, with public transport covered only roughly. This project built more flexible, map-based tools to fill that gap.

title: Street-level carbon footprint of urban transport in Poland
text:
What I did

1. Turned handwritten traffic logs into data
I digitised 180 handwritten traffic records from Warsaw bus stops (line, arrival time, vehicle and passengers boarding or leaving) with AI support. I cleaned them into structured files, then wrote an R script to calculate total and average occupancy and map it as a heatmap by line and hour.



From handwritten logs to a clean dataset and an occupancy heatmap by bus line and hour




2. Mapped road emissions street by street
Using the city’s GHG inventory, I mapped emissions for each road segment in Poznań, then applied the same method to Wrocław and Kraków:

downloaded city boundaries and road networks from OpenStreetMap and Geoportal
extracted the city road layer in QGIS
merged road geometry with emission data in R, after standardising Polish street names and characters
produced emission intensity maps in QGIS

The Poznań results use the Institute’s internal data and are kept confidential.


3. Built an R model for public transport emissions
Because the inventory paid little attention to buses, I built a new R model for Warsaw’s public transport. It combines official GTFS timetable data from ZTM Warszawa with OpenStreetMap streets. I focused on one major corridor, Aleje Jerozolimskie, and the bus lines crossing it.



Warsaw bus routes (blue) crossing the selected corridor, Aleje Jerozolimskie (red)


For each route segment, the model calculates length and travel time (at an average 18 km/h), applies emission factors for CO₂, NOx and PM10, and sums emissions per route and as CO₂-equivalent.






NOx emission intensity







PM10 emission intensity









CO₂ emission intensity







CO₂-equivalent emission intensity

title: Street-level carbon footprint of urban transport in Poland
text:
Key findings

Emissions are concentrated on major corridors, not spread evenly across the city
High-capacity roads tend to carry more traffic and produce more emissions
Emission maps reveal real hotspots, allowing more targeted policies
Data quality is the main bottleneck: encoding errors, inconsistent street names and gaps between datasets meant about 80% of Poznań’s roads could be matched and mapped, so data standardisation is essential

title: Street-level carbon footprint of urban transport in Poland
text:
Contributions to the Institute

A new R-based modelling framework that goes beyond Excel tools
A reproducible GIS method for street-level emission mapping
A list of key data gaps to fix
Evidence to support policies such as targeting high-emission roads, improving public transport planning and strengthening data systems

title: Street-level carbon footprint of urban transport in Poland
text:
Limitations
The public transport model is a simplified (Tier 1) approach. It assumes constant speed and a linear link between distance and emissions, and does not yet distinguish vehicle types, fuels (diesel vs. electric), stop-and-go driving or congestion. A natural next step is to use emission factors from the EMEP/EEA guidebook.

title: Son My 2 LNG-to-Power Project
text:
Overview
Son My 2 is a 2,250 MW LNG-fired combined cycle power plant planned within the Son My Power Centre on the south-central coast of Vietnam. The site was originally planned for coal power and was later redesigned as two gas-fired plants, Son My 1 and Son My 2. Fuel will come from the neighbouring Son My LNG import terminal, which is being developed by AES and PetroVietnam Gas (PV Gas) and is sized to supply up to 4,500 MW of gas-fired generation. Together, the plant and terminal are intended to diversify Vietnam’s energy mix with imported LNG and meet growing electricity demand.
